name: L-carnitine and acetyl-L-carnitine
short: In neuropathy trials, adverse events with acetyl-L-carnitine were similar to placebo; L-carnitine taken for 12 to 24 weeks raised blood TMAO, a compound linked to atherosclerosis.
text: In a meta-analysis of randomized trials of acetyl-L-carnitine for nerve pain, no severe related adverse events were reported and total adverse event rates were similar to control; common events included pain, headache, tingling (paraesthesia), retching, biliary colic and gastrointestinal disorders. A systematic review of L-carnitine supplementation for 12 to 24 weeks in healthy people found it raised fasting blood levels of trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), a compound thought to be pro-atherogenic, and called for longer-term cardiovascular studies. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.

quotes: No severe adverse events were reported related to ALC. The common adverse events were pain, headache, paraesthesia, hyperesthesia, retching, biliary colic, and gastrointestinal disorders. The rates of total adverse events were similar in ALC and control group.
citations.label: Li et al., 2015, PLoS One
citations.title: Acetyl-L-carnitine in the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

quotes: All the selected studies were conducted with healthy human subjects, with supplemented dose ranging from 1 g to 4 g per day for either 12 or 24 weeks.

LC supplementation elevates fasting plasma TMAO, compound supposed to be pro-atherogenic. Therefore, additional studies focusing on long-term supplementation and its longitudinal effect on the cardiovascular system are needed.
citations.label: Sawicka et al., 2020, J Int Soc Sports Nutr
citations.title: The bright and the dark sides of L-carnitine supplementation: a systematic review.
